title: Standard deviation versus standard error
dek: SD describes scatter of the observations (or of a named random variable). SE describes scatter of an estimator under replication. One is about Y; the other is about θ̂.
story: The standard deviation of Y is √Var(Y): how far a new draw of the same random variable tends to sit from E[Y]. A lab SD of log MIC describes assay-plus-biology scatter. It does not shrink just because you typed n into software.

The standard error of an estimator θ̂ is √Var(θ̂), usually estimated. For the iid sample mean, se(Ȳ) = s/√n. Replication shrinks the SE; it does not shrink the SD of a single patient’s MIC. Error bars that hide which of the two you plotted are how “the effect got more precise” becomes “the biology got quieter.”

A confidence interval uses an SE (or a likelihood root, or a bootstrap SD of θ̂). A reference range uses an SD of Y. Publishing Ȳ ± s as if it were a 95% CI for μ is the classic swap: you have drawn a band that should cover about 68% of new observations, not 95% of the mean.
deepTitle: What to print, and what dependence does to both
deep: s = √(∑ (yᵢ − ȳ)² / (n − 1)) estimates σ = sd(Y), not se(Ȳ). Always divide by √n (and apply a design factor) when the target is the mean.

Software labels lie. A GLM “Std. Error” is an SE of a coefficient. A column titled SD in a table of district rates might be an SD of ȳⱼ across districts (a between-unit SD) or an SE of one ȳⱼ. Caption the object.

Clustered data: the SD of Y can stay honest as a descriptive of person-level scatter while the SE of a mean must include the intraclass correlation. Using s/√n on 400 household members from 40 houses understates se(Ȳ).
Bootstrap and sandwich estimates are recipes for se(θ̂) when a model-based formula is untrusted. They still estimate a sampling SD of an estimator, not sd(Y).
Bayesian posterior SD is a different third object: a posterior width for θ, not a sampling SE, unless you have a matching Bernstein–von Mises story. Do not caption it as “the SE.”

formulas.label: iid SE of the mean

example.title: Error bars on a four-lab MIC mean
example.setup: Four labs each report one log-MIC for a wild-type QC strain: 0.1, 0.3, 0.0, 0.4. Sample SD s ≈ 0.183. A slide plots ȳ = 0.20 with whiskers ±s. A reviewer asks whether this is a CI for the mean log-MIC.

steps.title: Name the two widths
steps.body: s ≈ 0.183 is an SD of lab-level Y. se(Ȳ) = 0.183/√4 ≈ 0.091. A crude 95% interval for the mean would use the SE (and a t₃ reference, even), not ±s.

steps.title: What ±s actually covers
steps.body: ȳ ± s is a descriptive band for lab scatter, roughly a 68% reference range if Gaussian — not a 95% CI for μ. The slide overstated precision of the mean by a factor of two and mislabelled the object.

steps.title: If labs are the population
steps.body: If the scientific target is “how much do these four labs disagree?”, plot the four points and quote s. If the target is “what is the QC mean?”, plot ȳ with an SE or a posterior SD and say which.

example.takeaway: Whiskers need a noun: SD of Y, or SE of θ̂. The √n is the test.

choices: The SD of a single new observation Y
An (estimated) standard deviation of an estimator θ̂ under replication
check.answer: An (estimated) standard deviation of an estimator θ̂ under replication
check.why: SE lives on the sampling law of the estimator. SD lives on Y (or another named random variable).

whyWrong.Always s, regardless of n: s estimates sd(Y); se(Ȳ) divides by √n.
whyWrong.A posterior probability: A posterior SD is a third object and is not a probability.

whyWrong.0.5: That is 8/16, dividing by n not √n.

check.prompt: On the small-multiples plate, which width is supposed to shrink when n grows?
check.figureHint: Left panel flat; right panel shorter at n=16.
check.why: Var(Ȳ) = σ²/n under iid. sd(Y) is a property of one draw of Y.

whyWrong.sd(Y): The left panel is drawn n-invariant on purpose.
whyWrong.Both, equally: Only the estimator’s sampling SD shrinks like 1/√n.
